summary: This layer checks the 75 cases with killings or shootings that were on the map when it had 290 cases against IMF lending histories, the World Bank project database and IFC, MIGA and CAO records. 72 cases have a dated killing; where sources give only a month or a span of days, the count starts from the last possible day. title: When a deal ended or changed, the company sued the state
summary: Foreign companies that bought or ran privatized water, gas and power services, or held mining rights, have used investment treaties to sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts, took services back or stopped a deal, including when protests forced it. Most of these claims went to ICSID, the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes in Washington, which its own website calls "one of the five organizations of the World Bank Group". The legal basis was usually a bilateral investment treaty, an agreement between two countries that lets a company from one sue the other.

title: Where the companies come from
summary: This map's own count, from the companies named in the 290 cases it had when this was counted. 151 cases name at least one company, in 297 company roles (owner, operator, contractor or buyer). 173 of those roles (58%) belong to companies based outside the country where the harm happened. Of these foreign roles, 140 (81%) belong to companies based in today's high-income countries and 96 (55%) to companies based in the G7 (the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Canada, Italy, Germany and Japan). title: Aid money that goes back to companies in the donor country
summary:
Tied aid is aid that must be spent on goods or services from the country that gave it. Eurodad, a European network of groups working on debt and aid, counted about $26.9 billion of tied aid in 2018, or 21% of bilateral and EU aid. Its total for formal and informal tying together is at least $32.3 billion and possibly up to $37.9 billion. It puts the direct short-term cost of tying at $2 billion to $7 billion.

title: Aid that rises and falls with votes at the UN
summary: Two studies measure aid against UN politics. Kuziemko and Werker (Journal of Political Economy, 2006) studied developing countries, using US aid data for 1946-2001 and UN aid data for 1960-2001. They find that when a country rotates onto the UN Security Council, its US aid rises 59% and its UN aid 8%. Aid rises sharply in the year of election and returns to its earlier level almost immediately after the term ends; UN aid takes until the second year after. title: Funds that buy old debt and sue in New York and London
summary:
When a country cannot pay, most lenders usually accept a reduced deal. A holdout refuses and sues for the full amount. A vulture fund is the critics' name for a fund that buys defaulted debt to do this. An ECB working paper (no. 2135, 2018) by Schumacher, Trebesch and Enderlein counted 158 cases against 34 defaulting governments from 1976 to 2010: 130 in US courts (82.3%), 23 in the UK (14.6%) and 5 in arbitration. New York law governs almost half of outstanding sovereign bonds (White & Case, 2024) or over 50% (Insurance Journal, 2026).

title: Who holds the debt, and the rich-country law it runs under
summary:
Debt Justice, a UK campaign group, counted $900 billion in external debt payments by 88 lower-income countries for 2020 to 2025, using World Bank data. Private lenders other than Chinese ones got 39% ($354 billion), multilateral lenders 34% ($304 billion), other governments 14% ($125 billion) and Chinese public and private lenders 13% ($117 billion). The amounts for 2020-2023 are payments made. The amounts for 2024 and 2025 are scheduled payments on debts contracted by the end of 2023, not payments made, and leave out loans taken since then.

title: Secrecy and security in Chinese loan contracts
summary: In 2021 AidData and its co-authors (Gelpern, Horn, Morris, Parks and Trebesch) published 100 contracts between Chinese state-owned lenders and governments in 24 developing countries, with a dataset of $36.6 billion in loans from 2000 to 2020. They report "unusual confidentiality clauses that bar borrowers from revealing the terms or even the existence of the debt," and security such as "lender-controlled revenue accounts." title: Debt relief: the Paris Club, China and who goes first
summary: The Paris Club is an informal group of creditor governments, dating to 1956, that reschedules loans together, case by case and tied to an IMF-backed programme. Lex Rieffel, a former US Treasury desk officer for it, writes that "China, however, is not a member," and lists it among ad hoc participants. He cites a study by Horn, Reinhart and Trebesch putting debt owed to China at $370 billion at end-2017, against $246 billion owed to the 22 Paris Club members. title: How much foreign investors take home, and to which countries
summary:
Foreign direct investment earns income for its owners, and part stays in the host country. UNCTAD, the UN trade and development body, reports $1.5 trillion of this income in 2011 on $21 trillion of investment, a 7% return: 8% in developing economies, 13% in transition economies and 5% in developed countries. Globally in 2011, nearly one-third stayed in host economies and two-thirds went back to investors.

title: Investment routed through tax havens, and the tax that goes missing
summary: UNCTAD said in 2015 that about 30% of cross-border corporate investment passes through offshore hubs, and estimated developing countries lose about $100 billion a year in tax on investment linked to those hubs. Across developing economies, each 10 percentage points of offshore investment goes with a 1-point lower rate of return. IMF economists Damgaard, Elkjaer and Johannesen wrote in 2019 that phantom investment, money passing through empty companies, comes to $15 trillion, almost 40% of global FDI, up from about 30% less than a decade earlier. title: Donors decide what most of the money given to UN bodies pays for
summary: A government can give a UN body or other multilateral organisation "core" money, which the organisation decides how to spend, or "earmarked" money, which the donor ties to a country, topic or project. The Financing the UN Development System report (Dag Hammarskjöld Foundation and UN MPTF Office, 2025) says earmarked money rose from 51% of all UN system funding in 2010 to 61% in 2023. In dollars that is $20.3 billion to $41 billion, down from $49.6 billion in 2022. Voluntary core money was $5.7 billion in 2023.
